subject: chemistry
title: Period 3 oxides and chlorides
key_idea: Period 3 elements form oxides that change from basic to amphoteric to acidic. The change follows bonding: ionic oxides give alkaline solutions, covalent oxides give acidic ones. Chlorides follow the same pattern, with covalent ones hydrolysed by water.

blocks.text: Sodium to sulfur react with oxygen and chlorine, and sodium and magnesium react with water. This section covers each reaction and the products.

items: Sodium reacts vigorously with cold water. It melts, fizzes and moves on the surface.
Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water but burns in steam.
The others do not react with water.
Sodium burns with a yellow flame. Magnesium burns with a bright white flame. Sulfur burns with a blue flame.
Sulfur dioxide is oxidised to SO₃ only with a catalyst and heat: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃.
Phosphorus forms PCl₅ in excess chlorine.
Na and Mg react with water to give hydroxides and hydrogen.
Each element burns in oxygen to form its oxide.
Each of Na, Mg, Al, Si and P forms a chloride with chlorine.

sections.heading: Oxides with water: pH and acid–base behaviour

blocks.text: The oxides change from basic to acidic across the period. This section covers what each does with water, acids and bases.

items.meaning: Reacts with both acids and bases.
Reacts with acids to form a salt and water.
Reacts with bases to form a salt and water.

blocks.text: Basic oxides react with acids. Acidic oxides react with bases. Aluminium oxide reacts with both.
Mg(OH)₂ is basic. Al(OH)₃ is amphoteric: it dissolves in acid and in excess sodium hydroxide. NaOH is a strong base.

options.label: Al₂O₃
results: Giant ionic with some covalent character

items: Oxides go from basic (Na₂O, MgO) through amphoteric (Al₂O₃) to acidic (SiO₂ to SO₃).
Ionic oxides that dissolve give alkaline solutions. Covalent oxides that react give acidic solutions.
Al₂O₃ and Al(OH)₃ dissolve in both acid and alkali.

sections.heading: Why the pattern changes: bonding and electronegativity

blocks.text: Bonding moves from ionic to covalent across the period. This section covers why, and how to work out the bonding from a property.

items: Oxygen and chlorine are very electronegative. Sodium and magnesium are not, so the electronegativity difference is large and the bonding is **ionic**.
The difference shrinks across the period. Al₂O₃ and AlCl₃ show covalent character, and SiO₂ and SiCl₄ are covalent.
Ionic oxides contain O²⁻ ions, which accept H⁺ from water to form OH⁻. So they are basic.
Covalent oxides of non-metals react with water to form acids, which release H⁺.

rows: High melting point, conducts when molten
Dissolves to a neutral or alkaline solution
Low melting point, does not conduct
Fumes and gives an acidic solution with water

items: The electronegativity difference with O or Cl decreases across the period.
Ionic compounds give basic or neutral solutions. Covalent compounds give acidic solutions.
Use melting point, conductivity and the pH of the solution to work out the bonding.

checks.q: Write the equation for the reaction of sodium with water and state the pH of the solution formed.
checks.a: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. The pH is about 13 to 14.

checks.q: Aluminium oxide is amphoteric. Write an equation for its reaction with hydrochloric acid, and say what shows it is amphoteric.
checks.a: Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O. It is amphoteric because it also reacts with sodium hydroxide, so it reacts with both acid and base.

checks.q: Explain why phosphorus(V) oxide gives an acidic solution but sodium oxide gives an alkaline one.
checks.a: Na₂O is ionic and contains O²⁻ ions, which react with water to form OH⁻. P₄O₁₀ is a covalent non-metal oxide that reacts with water to form H₃PO₄, which releases H⁺.

blocks.text: This part covers the melting points of the highest oxides and the acids and anions formed from the acidic oxides.

items: Na₂O, MgO and Al₂O₃ have high melting points because the ionic lattice has strong attraction between ions. MgO is the highest of the three, as Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ are small and doubly charged.
SiO₂ has a very high melting point because it is a giant covalent lattice with strong bonds throughout.
P₄O₁₀, SO₂ and SO₃ have low melting points. They are simple molecules with weak London forces between them.
The trend: high for the giant oxides Na₂O to SiO₂, then a sharp fall to the molecular oxides.
H₃PO₄: P bonded to one O by a double bond and to three OH groups.
H₂SO₄: S bonded to two O by double bonds and to two OH groups.
H₂SO₃: S bonded to one O by a double bond and to two OH groups, with a lone pair.

blocks.text: In each acid the central atom is bonded to O atoms, and the OH groups lose H⁺. The anions are tetrahedral for PO₄³⁻ and SO₄²⁻, and pyramidal for SO₃²⁻.
This part covers oxidation numbers and the reactions of the chlorides with water.

items: The oxidation number rises as the number of outer-shell (valence) electrons used rises, from 1 for Na to 5 for P.
Sulfur has 6 valence electrons. It uses 4 in SO₂ and all 6 in SO₃.
Chlorine in a chloride stays at −1.
NaCl and MgCl₂ are ionic and dissolve. The ions are hydrated but the chloride ions do not react.
AlCl₃, SiCl₄ and PCl₅ are covalent and hydrolysed. They give fumes of hydrogen chloride and an acidic solution.
Al³⁺ is a small, highly charged ion, so it polarises water and releases H⁺ in solution.
